chunks: Roles of boost diode, inductor, capacitor. The question: What is the purpose of the diode? The inductor? The capacitor?
Each of the three main boost parts has one job. The inductor stores energy and pushes it out at a higher voltage.
The diode is a one-way valve that sends that energy to the output and stops the output from draining back.
The capacitor holds the output steady, because it alone supplies the load while the switch is on.
Imagine a pump system. The inductor is a heavy pump wheel that builds up momentum. The diode is a check valve, so water flows only toward the tank.
The capacitor is the tank, which keeps the taps running while the wheel is being spun up again. If you remove the check valve, the tank empties backward.
The analogy does not show the real parts' limits, such as how much current the wheel can handle before saturating.
The inductor (blue) is the only energy-storing path. The diode (red) is the only route from the switch node to the output.
The capacitor (green) is the only thing holding the output between diode pulses. Remove any one and the circuit stops being a boost.
Inductor: stores energy in a magnetic field. Its value sets the ripple current ("What a boost converter is").
Schottky diode: a one-way valve that wastes only a small voltage (about 0. 4 volts) while it conducts. Output capacitor: holds up the output voltage between pulses.
Ripple: the small repeating variation in current or voltage. Saturation current: the current at which the inductor stops working properly.
Say the converter runs at 5 volts in, 10 volts out, 1 amps load, 500 kilohertz and D equals 0. 5 .
During the 1 microseconds on-time, the diode blocks and the capacitor alone supplies 1 amps.
With a 22 microfarads capacitor the output droops by about 1 amps times 1 micro s over 22 micro F about 45 millivolts.
In the off-time, the inductor refills the capacitor through the diode. That is the whole idea.
"The inductor is the energy store: it charges while the switch is on and then forces its current into the output when the switch opens, which is what lifts the voltage.
The diode is the one-way valve: it carries the inductor current to the output in the off-time and blocks in the on-time so the output capacitor isn't shorted to ground.
The capacitor holds the output steady: it supplies the load during the on-time and smooths the pulsed diode current, and it sets the output ripple."
